L,D-transpeptides are essential for peptido-glycan cross-linkage in Enterococcus and that L,D-trans- peptides can be targeted by β-lactam antibiotics.

the slow acylation of the β-lacatamase Ldtfm and slow acylation of Ldtfm by the β-lactams ampicillin and cephalosporin Ceftriaxion are responsible for the high MIC of E. faecium resistant to ampicillin.
the slow inactivation by ceftriaxon and ampicillin of the L,D-transpeptides is due to the slow acylation step of the catalysis and the fast hydrolysis of the acylenzymes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel β-lactam antibiotics that can overcome the resistance to β-lacatams conferred by the L,D-transpeptide.
the development of novel antibiotics to treat infections caused by multidrug resistant bacteria.
the molecular mechanism of the L,D-Transpetidases (Ldt) and the development of new β-lactam antibiotics that are active against L,D-Transptidases.

the L,D-transpepidase is not the target for the carbapenems, but the carbapenams are the target for the L,D-transpedidase.

the β-lactams that are active against the L,D-transpepeptidase Ldtfm have the following characteristics: 1) a β-lactam carbonyl that forms an efficient covalent acylenzymes with Ldtfm; 2) an oxyanion that is stabilized by the β-lactamate ring and 3) a C5–C7 bond that can be easily cleaved.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the oxyanion and the acylenzymes are the key intermediates of the catalytic pathway for β-lactam antibiotics.

the oxyanion and the acylenzymes formed by β-lactams in their reaction with L,D-transpeptides must be efficiently trapped in order to ensure rapid inactivation of L,D-transpeptide and efficient antibacterial activity.
Ldtfm is a new target for β-lactams.
